5- Calcul des coefficients de pondération (cliquez sur chaque carte pour afficher l'input et l'output)

Input — Projections de la population établies selon les résultats du recensement

4 dimensions — Région, Milieu de résidence, Sexe, Âge groupé

Date de référence — Date du trimestre

Méthode — Régression linéaire

Output — Population du trimestre

Input — Enregistrements de personnes

Étape permettant d'évaluer la non réponse totale en termes de ménages dans chaque UP

Output — Nombre de ménages enquêtés par UP

Input — Nombre de ménages enquêtés par UP

Objectif — Chaque UP, chaque strate d'habitat, chaque province est représentée en termes de ménages fidèlement au plan de sondage

But — Chaque UP est représentée par 20 ménages

Cible — Pallier la non réponse totale dans les UP où moins de 20 ménages ont été enquêtés

Méthode — Post stratification

Output — Coefficients de redressement primaires

Inputs — Coefficients de pondération de base, Coefficients de redressement primaires

Appliquer les coefficients de redressement primaires aux coefficients de pondération de base

Output — Coefficients de pondération intermédiaires

Inputs — Enregistrements de personnes, Coefficients de pondération intermédiaires

4 dimensions — Région, Milieu de résidence, Sexe, Âge groupé

Outputs — Population enquêtée pondérée par les coefficients de pondération intermédiaires

Inputs — Population enquêtée pondérée par les coefficients de pondération intermédiaires, Population du trimestre

Objectif — Chaque groupe de la population enquêtée est représenté fidèlement à la distribution de la population projetée

Cible — Pallier la sur représentativité et la sous représentativité des différents groupes de la population enquêtée

Méthode — Post stratification

280 contraintes (trimestre) — 322 contraintes (année)

Output — Coefficients de redressement secondaires

Inputs — Coefficients de pondération intermédiaires, Coefficients de redressement secondaires

Appliquer les coefficients de redressement secondaires aux coefficients de pondération intermédiaires

Output — Coefficients de pondération finaux

Objectif — Évaluer la qualité du redressement

Inputs — Coefficients de pondération (de base, intermédiaires, finaux), Coefficients de redressement (primaires, secondaires, globaux)

Outputs — Statistiques descriptives des différents coefficients de pondération et des différents coefficients de redressement, Tabulation de la population selon les 4 dimensions

Exemple de script SPSS — Calcul des coefficients de pondération

▶ Voir le script complet 
* Encoding: UTF-8.
dataset name DATA.

* !! 3 PARAMETRES (TAB) !! Chargement des projections de la population par région et par milieu de résidence.
*the parent population.
get data
/type=xlsx
    /file="C:\Users\zarou\Desktop\ENE SPSS\Les projections de la population par région et par milieu de résidence.xlsx"
    /sheet=name "2022T3"
/cellrange=range "A1:C21"
/readnames=on
/datatypemin percentage=95.0 
/hidden ignore=yes.
exe.
dataset name PROJ window=front.
dataset activate PROJ.
sort cases by REGION10 MILIEU.
variable labels REGION10 "Région" MILIEU "Milieu de résidence" POP.PROJ "Population projetée par région et par milieu de résidence".
formats MILIEU (f1) REGION10 (f2) POP.PROJ (f7.2).
    save outfile="C:\Users\zarou\Desktop\ENE SPSS\Projections de la population par région et par milieu de résidence.sav"
/compressed.
dataset close PROJ.
dataset activate DATA. 

* !! 1 PARAMETRE (TAB) !! Ajout des projections de la population par région et par milieu de résidence.
*chque membre a sa population cible correspondante.
sort cases by REGION10 MILIEU.
match files /file=*
    /table="C:\Users\zarou\Desktop\ENE SPSS\Projections de la population par région et par milieu de résidence.sav"
/by REGION10 MILIEU.
exe.

*astuce classique pr compter le nbre de ménage à partir des données indiv. 
*Identification du premier membre de chaque ménage.
*jutilise match files pr garder les memes lignes et creer une var de position /first.
sort cases by UP MENAGE.
match files
/file=*
/by UP MENAGE
/first=MEM1.MEN.
exe.

*Calcul du nombre de ménages enquêtés par UP.
*on doit enquêter 20 mng par UP.
aggregate 
/outfile=* mode=addvariables 
/break=UP
/NB.MEN.UP=SUM(MEM1.MEN).
delete variables MEM1.MEN.
variable labels NB.MEN.UP "Nombre de ménages enquêtés par UP".
variable level NB.MEN.UP (scale).
formats NB.MEN.UP (f2).

*Afficher nbr de ménage par UP.
ctables
    /table UP [C]  > NB.MEN.UP [MEAN].

 *we use aggregate if we want to add a new var otherwise we use match files / file=*.

*Calcul des coefficients de redressement primaires.
compute COEF.RED1 = 20 / NB.MEN.UP.
exe.
variable labels COEF.RED1 "Coefficient de redressement primaire".
variable level COEF.RED1 (scale).
formats COEF.RED1 (f3.2).

*Redressement des coefficients de pondération de base (pour que chaque UP soit représentée par 20 ménages).
*le redressement agit comme un facteur dajustement cest pr ca on multiplie.
*pds.trim.base issue de lechantillonage cest linverse de la probabilité d'inclusion.
*le poids n'est pas encore final il est :corrigé au niveau UP mais pas encore calé sur la population.
compute PDS.TRIM.INT=PDS.TRIM.BASE * COEF.RED1.
exe.
variable labels PDS.TRIM.INT "Coefficient de pondération trimestriel intermédiaire".
variable level PDS.TRIM.INT (scale).
formats PDS.TRIM.INT (f4.2).

*Calcul de la population enquêtée pondérée par région et par milieu de résidence.
*weight by: a partir de mnt chaque indiv compte pds.trim.int individus.
*weight off: les prochaines analyses ne seront plus pondérées.
weight by PDS.TRIM.INT.
aggregate
/outfile=* mode=addvariables
/break=REGION10 MILIEU
/POP.ENQ.PND.INT=n.
weight off.
variable labels POP.ENQ.PND.INT "Population enquêtée pondérée (avec le poids intermédiaire) par région et par milieu de résidence".
variable level POP.ENQ.PND.INT (scale).
formats POP.ENQ.PND.INT (f7.2).
*Affichage de population enquetee ponderee.
ctables
    /table MILIEU  > REGION10  > POP.ENQ.PND.INT [MEAN F12.0].

*Calcul des coefficients de redressement secondaires : calage.
compute COEF.RED2 = POP.PROJ / POP.ENQ.PND.INT.
variable labels COEF.RED2 "Coefficient de redressement secondaire".
variable level COEF.RED2 (scale).
formats COEF.RED2 (f3.2).

*Redressement des coefficients de pondération intermédiaires.
compute PDS.TRIM = PDS.TRIM.INT * COEF.RED2.
exe.
variable labels PDS.TRIM "Coefficient de pondération trimestriel de la personne".
variable level PDS.TRIM (scale).
formats PDS.TRIM (f4.2).

*Tri initial.
sort cases by MOIS REGION UP MENAGE MEMBRE.

*Tabulation pour vérification de la conformité avec les projections de la population.
*ctables custom table to create cross tabulation table.
*milieu in rows and region10 in columns >  means nesting/crossing.
*comma40.0 thoousands seperators with field 40 and 0 digits.
*statistical labels no visible make the table cleaner. 
*Après pondération le nombre de personnes estimé dans chaque combinaison Région × Milieu doit être égal (ou quasiment égal) à la valeur POP PROJ du fichier de projections C'est une étape de contrôle qualité. 
*si les totaux ne correspondent pas, cela signifie que le calage n'a pas été correctement appliqué.
*Verifier si pop.proj = pop enquetee ponderee.
weight by PDS.TRIM.
ctables 
/table MILIEU > REGION10 [count comma40.0]
/slabels visible=no
/criteria cilevel=95.
weight off.
 
*Calcul des statistiques d'évaluation du redressement.
compute COEF.RED.GLOB = PDS.TRIM / PDS.TRIM.BASE.
exe.
variable labels COEF.RED.GLOB "Coefficient de redressement global".
variable level COEF.RED.GLOB (scale).
formats COEF.RED.GLOB (f3.2).
ctables
/table AN > TRIM > (PDS.TRIM.BASE + NB.MEN.UP + COEF.RED1 + PDS.TRIM.INT + COEF.RED2 + PDS.TRIM + COEF.RED.GLOB) [MEAN, STDDEV, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM].

*Suppression des variables intermédiaires.
delete variables  POP.ENQ.PND.INT.

*COEF.RED1 corrige un problème d'échantillonnage sur le terrain (certaines UP n'ont pas exactement 20 ménages).
*COEF.RED2 corrige un écart entre l'échantillon et la population officielle projetée (le calage).
delete variables POP.PROJ NB.MEN.UP first.UP COEF.RED1 PDS.TRIM.INT COEF.RED2 PDS.TRIM COEF.RED.GLOB.

6- Interprétation des résultats de pondération

1- Coefficient de pondération trimestriel de base (PDS.TRIM.BASE)
Avant tout redressement, chaque individu représentait en moyenne 327 personnes de la population. En effet, les poids varient de 235 à 416, ce qui montre que certaines personnes avaient une probabilité d'inclusion plus faible que d'autres. Concernant l'écart-type (29,86), il reste relativement faible par rapport à la moyenne, ce qui indique que les poids de base sont assez homogènes. Par conséquent, les poids issus du plan de sondage sont cohérents et ne présentent pas de dispersion excessive.

2- Nombre de ménages enquêtés par UP
On prévoyait 20 ménages par UP. En moyenne, 19 ménages ont été effectivement enquêtés. Certaines UP ont atteint les 20 ménages prévus, tandis que d'autres n'en comptaient que 14, probablement en raison de refus, d'absences ou de logements inoccupés. Donc le taux de réalisation est globalement bon, mais quelques UP ont nécessité un ajustement.

3- Coefficient de redressement primaire (COEF.RED1)
Le coefficient corrige les écarts entre les 20 ménages prévus et le nombre réellement enquêté. Une moyenne de 1,04 signifie que les poids ont été augmentés en moyenne de 4 %. Le minimum est 1, ce qui correspond aux UP où les 20 ménages ont bien été enquêtés. Le maximum de 1,43 correspond aux UP ayant seulement 14 ménages. Par conséquent, le redressement primaire est faible et reflète uniquement les pertes de ménages observées sur le terrain.

4- Coefficient de pondération trimestriel intermédiaire (PDS.TRIM.INT)
Ce poids est obtenu après application du premier redressement, la moyenne est passée de 327 à 339, ce qui est logique puisque le redressement primaire est supérieur à 1. Les poids ont augmenté légèrement afin de compenser les ménages manquants. On remarque que les poids intermédiaires sont homogènes et l'effet du redressement primaire est limité.

5- Coefficient de redressement secondaire (COEF.RED2)
Ce coefficient théoriquement devrait être proche de 1 pour juger avoir réalisé un bon ajustement, mais vu que les données sont synthétiques ici, il est en moyenne de 96,26, ce qui est beaucoup plus élevé que dans un calage dont nous avons l'habitude de réaliser.

6- Coefficient de pondération trimestriel de la personne (PDS.TRIM)
Les poids varient entre 14 386 et 86 333 personnes selon la région, le milieu de résidence et les probabilités d'inclusion. Ceci résulte du coefficient de redressement secondaire qui est très élevé aussi et comme il est déjà mentionné, c'est un résultat qui est à l'origine de la nature des données utilisées pour présenter ce projet. Cependant, théoriquement, ces poids permettent de produire des estimations représentatives de la population.

1- Projet de produits

Cette étape consiste à préparer les données en vue de la tabulation :

  • Nettoyage des données et règlement des problèmes détectés a posteriori, notamment les données manquantes, les valeurs extrêmes, les variables présentant des structures inhabituelles, ainsi que les variables comportant un nombre élevé de réponses de type « autre »
  • Élaboration de la tabulation, notamment le calcul des variables, l'utilisation des coefficients de pondération appropriés, l'application des filtres adaptés à chaque catégorie, ainsi que le choix des variables à inclure dans l'analyse et de celles à reporter en annexe
  • Production des tableaux

2- Validation des produits

Étude de vraisemblance :

  • Comparer les statistiques aux cycles précédents, en vérifiant la tendance des indicateurs produits par rapport aux mêmes indicateurs des années précédentes
  • Confronter les statistiques à d'autres données pertinentes, internes et externes, afin de s'assurer de la vraisemblance des résultats en conformité avec la conjoncture nationale et internationale
  • Vérifier la conformité des résultats à la conjoncture nationale, notamment au regard des données sectorielles (campagne agricole, tourisme, BTP, industrie…)
  • Vérifier la conformité des résultats à la conjoncture internationale, en tenant compte de l'impact des crises en général (ex. Covid)
  • Ventilation des données

3- Interprétation et explication des produits

  • Choix des variables à inclure dans l'analyse
  • Choix des méthodes d'analyse :
    • Descriptive
    • Explicative
    • Prédictive
    Au niveau de l'enquête, on penche vers l'analyse descriptive
  • Analyse des séries temporelles de données :
    • Prendre en compte les changements méthodologiques introduits au cours de la période (définition, base de sondage…)
    • Glissement annuel ou entre deux périodes successives : correction de la variation saisonnière
  • Analyse progressive dépend du calendrier de diffusion :
    • 1ère phase : analyse des indicateurs phares avec un nombre limité de ventilation, exemple :
      • Création de l'emploi (total, milieu, secteur et type d'emploi)
      • Tendances de l'activité et emploi (total, milieu, sexe et âge)
      • Tendances de chômage (total, milieu, sexe, âge et diplôme)
      • Tendances du sous-emploi (total, milieu et secteur)
    • 2ème phase : analyse avec focus sur certaines catégories
    • 3ème phase : analyse d'un nombre plus important d'indicateurs et une ventilation plus détaillée

4- Contrôle et Divulgation

  • Évaluation de la ventilation utilisée pour éviter toute divulgation d'informations sensibles
  • Contrôle de la divulgation des micro-données (anonymisation)

5- Publications

  • Marché du travail — Publications
  • Plateforme « Le marché du travail en chiffres » — visuels interactifs
  • Plateforme « ODD 8 relatif au marché du travail »
  • Situation du marché du travail au T1-2026 après la réforme de l'enquête

Montreal Real Estate Analytics: Price Prediction & Portfolio Segmentation

Synthetic dataset generation Relatively realistic to Montreal Real estate market
Data Preparation
Predictive Modeling and Portfolio Understanding
Evaluation & Optimization
Property segmentation
Business Outcome

The dataset used in this project is synthetic, generated with a Python script rather than collected from real transactions, but it was built to stay relatively realistic to the Montreal real estate market: the neighborhoods used are actual Montreal boroughs/areas, the property types reflect the terminology and mix typical of the Quebec market, and prices were calibrated to roughly match real-world magnitudes by neighborhood and property type.

Metadata

The sample contains 2,505 properties (rows), each described by 20 variables: 1 target variable and 19 explanatory variables.

Variable Type Meaning
PropertyIDIdentifierUnique ID assigned to each property listing (e.g., MTL-100779)
NeighborhoodCategorical (12 categories)Montreal-area borough where the property is located: Westmount, Outremont, Le Plateau-Mont-Royal, Ville-Marie (Downtown), Griffintown, Verdun, Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, NDG, Ahuntsic-Cartierville, Laval, Longueuil, Saint-Laurent
PropertyTypeCategorical (6 categories)Type of property: Condo, Detached, Semi-Detached, Duplex, Triplex, Townhouse
BedroomsNumerical (discrete)Number of bedrooms
BathroomsNumerical (continuous)Number of bathrooms (fractional values like 2.5 represent a half-bath)
LivingAreaSqFtNumerical (continuous)Interior living area, in square feet
LotSizeSqFtNumerical (continuous)Size of the land lot, in square feet (0 for condos, which don't own land)
YearBuiltNumerical (discrete)Year the property was originally constructed
RenovationYearNumerical (discrete)Year of the most recent renovation — missing (NaN) if the property was never renovated
GarageSpacesNumerical (discrete)Number of garage parking spaces (0-3)
HasBasementBinary (0/1)Whether the property has a basement
HasPoolBinary (0/1)Whether the property has a pool
ConditionCategorical (4 categories)Overall property condition: Poor, Fair, Good, Excellent
SchoolRatingNumerical (continuous)Rating of nearby schools, on a 0-10 scale
CrimeRatePer1000Numerical (continuous)Reported crime incidents per 1,000 residents in the neighborhood
DistanceToDowntownKmNumerical (continuous)Distance from the property to downtown Montreal, in kilometers
DaysOnMarketNumerical (discrete)Number of days the property was listed before it sold
SaleDateDateDate the sale closed (2021-2023)
AnnualPropertyTaxCADNumerical (continuous)Estimated annual municipal + school property tax, in CAD
SalePrice_CADNumerical (continuous) — target variableFinal sale price, in Canadian dollars — the value the regression model will predict
▶ View full script 
"""
Real Estate Data Project — synthetic data generator (Canadian / Montreal-area market)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Generates a realistic property portfolio dataset for the Montreal metropolitan
area, in CAD, with intentional data-quality issues (missing values, a few
outliers, duplicates) so the "Data Preparation" step has real work to do.

Output: data/real_estate_raw.csv
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

np.random.seed(42)

N = 2500  # number of properties

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Montreal-area neighborhoods/boroughs with different price tiers
#    (approximate relative price/sqft tiers in CAD, loosely reflecting
#    real Montreal market patterns)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
neighborhoods = {
    "Westmount":              {"base_price_sqft": 480, "school": (8, 10), "crime": (3, 10),  "dist": (2, 6)},
    "Outremont":               {"base_price_sqft": 460, "school": (8, 10), "crime": (3, 10),  "dist": (2, 6)},
    "Le Plateau-Mont-Royal":   {"base_price_sqft": 385, "school": (6, 9),  "crime": (10, 22), "dist": (1, 5)},
    "Ville-Marie (Downtown)":  {"base_price_sqft": 400, "school": (5, 8),  "crime": (18, 35), "dist": (0, 3)},
    "Griffintown":             {"base_price_sqft": 420, "school": (5, 8),  "crime": (12, 25), "dist": (1, 4)},
    "Verdun":                  {"base_price_sqft": 335, "school": (6, 9),  "crime": (8, 18),  "dist": (4, 9)},
    "Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie": {"base_price_sqft": 325, "school": (6, 9), "crime": (8, 20),  "dist": (4, 9)},
    "NDG (Notre-Dame-de-Grâce)": {"base_price_sqft": 315, "school": (7, 9), "crime": (6, 16),  "dist": (5, 10)},
    "Ahuntsic-Cartierville":   {"base_price_sqft": 285, "school": (6, 9),  "crime": (6, 16),  "dist": (7, 13)},
    "Laval":                   {"base_price_sqft": 250, "school": (6, 9),  "crime": (4, 12),  "dist": (12, 22)},
    "Longueuil":               {"base_price_sqft": 235, "school": (5, 8),  "crime": (5, 14),  "dist": (10, 20)},
    "Saint-Laurent":           {"base_price_sqft": 285, "school": (6, 9),  "crime": (5, 14),  "dist": (9, 16)},
}
nbhd_names = list(neighborhoods.keys())
nbhd_weights = [0.06, 0.05, 0.13, 0.10, 0.09, 0.09, 0.10, 0.09, 0.08, 0.09, 0.07, 0.05]

df = pd.DataFrame({"PropertyID": [f"MTL-{100000+i}" for i in range(N)]})
df["Neighborhood"] = np.random.choice(nbhd_names, size=N, p=nbhd_weights)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Property type — Canadian / Quebec terminology
#    (Duplex/Triplex are extremely common property types in Montreal)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
property_types = ["Condo", "Detached", "Semi-Detached", "Duplex", "Triplex", "Townhouse"]
type_weights = [0.34, 0.16, 0.12, 0.15, 0.10, 0.13]
df["PropertyType"] = np.random.choice(property_types, size=N, p=type_weights)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Structural attributes
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
def sample_bedrooms(ptype):
    if ptype == "Condo":
        return np.random.choice([1, 2, 3], p=[0.35, 0.45, 0.20])
    if ptype in ("Duplex", "Triplex"):
        return np.random.choice([3, 4, 5, 6], p=[0.25, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15])
    return np.random.choice([2, 3, 4, 5], p=[0.15, 0.40, 0.32, 0.13])

df["Bedrooms"] = df["PropertyType"].apply(sample_bedrooms)
df["Bathrooms"] = (df["Bedrooms"] * np.random.uniform(0.55, 0.9, N)).round(1).clip(1, 6)

def sample_living_area(row):
    base = {"Condo": 780, "Townhouse": 1350, "Semi-Detached": 1600,
            "Detached": 1900, "Duplex": 2400, "Triplex": 3200}[row["PropertyType"]]
    return max(400, int(np.random.normal(base + row["Bedrooms"] * 200, 320)))

df["LivingAreaSqFt"] = df.apply(sample_living_area, axis=1)
df["LotSizeSqFt"] = np.where(
    df["PropertyType"].isin(["Condo"]),
    0,
    (df["LivingAreaSqFt"] * np.random.uniform(1.1, 3.8, N)).astype(int)
)

df["YearBuilt"] = np.random.randint(1920, 2023, N)
df["GarageSpaces"] = np.random.choice([0, 1, 2, 3], size=N, p=[0.30, 0.35, 0.28, 0.07])  # street parking common in MTL
df["HasBasement"] = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=N, p=[0.35, 0.65])
df["HasPool"] = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=N, p=[0.93, 0.07])  # pools less common in Quebec

condition_labels = ["Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent"]
df["Condition"] = np.random.choice(condition_labels, size=N, p=[0.08, 0.27, 0.45, 0.20])

# Renovation: only ~35% of properties have ever been renovated —
# RenovationYear is *structurally* missing for the rest (not random noise).
renovated_mask = np.random.rand(N) < 0.35
df["RenovationYear"] = np.where(
    renovated_mask,
    np.random.randint(df["YearBuilt"].values, 2024),
    np.nan
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Location-driven features
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
def nbhd_school(row):
    lo, hi = neighborhoods[row["Neighborhood"]]["school"]
    return round(np.random.uniform(lo, hi), 1)

def nbhd_crime(row):
    lo, hi = neighborhoods[row["Neighborhood"]]["crime"]
    return round(np.random.uniform(lo, hi), 1)

def nbhd_dist(row):
    lo, hi = neighborhoods[row["Neighborhood"]]["dist"]
    return round(np.random.uniform(lo, hi), 1)

df["SchoolRating"] = df.apply(nbhd_school, axis=1)
df["CrimeRatePer1000"] = df.apply(nbhd_crime, axis=1)
df["DistanceToDowntownKm"] = df.apply(nbhd_dist, axis=1)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Market behavior
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
df["DaysOnMarket"] = np.random.negative_binomial(6, 0.15, N).clip(1, 400)
sale_dates = pd.date_range("2021-01-01", "2023-12-31", freq="D")
df["SaleDate"] = np.random.choice(sale_dates, N)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. SalePrice (CAD) — the target variable, built from a realistic formula + noise
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
condition_multiplier = {"Poor": 0.82, "Fair": 0.93, "Good": 1.0, "Excellent": 1.12}
type_price_multiplier = {"Condo": 1.30, "Townhouse": 1.0, "Semi-Detached": 0.95,
                          "Detached": 0.92, "Duplex": 0.72, "Triplex": 0.62}
current_year = 2024

def compute_price(row):
    base_sqft_price = neighborhoods[row["Neighborhood"]]["base_price_sqft"]
    price = row["LivingAreaSqFt"] * base_sqft_price * type_price_multiplier[row["PropertyType"]]
    price *= condition_multiplier[row["Condition"]]
    age = current_year - row["YearBuilt"]
    price *= (1 - min(age, 100) * 0.0022)
    if pd.notna(row["RenovationYear"]):
        years_since_reno = current_year - row["RenovationYear"]
        price *= (1 + max(0, (15 - years_since_reno)) * 0.006)
    price *= (1 + row["GarageSpaces"] * 0.025)
    price *= (1 + row["HasBasement"] * 0.035)
    price *= (1 + row["HasPool"] * 0.05)
    price *= (1 + (row["SchoolRating"] - 6) * 0.018)
    price *= (1 - (row["CrimeRatePer1000"] - 15) * 0.0035)
    price *= (1 - row["DistanceToDowntownKm"] * 0.0035)
    price += row["LotSizeSqFt"] * 2.5
    price *= np.random.normal(1.0, 0.07)  # market noise
    return max(price, 90000)

df["SalePrice_CAD"] = df.apply(compute_price, axis=1).round(-2).astype(int)

# Annual municipal + school property tax (Quebec municipalities typically
# assess ~0.7%-1.1% of property value annually)
df["AnnualPropertyTaxCAD"] = (df["SalePrice_CAD"] * np.random.uniform(0.007, 0.011, N)).round(-1).astype(int)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Inject realistic data-quality issues
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

def inject_missing(col, frac):
    idx = rng.choice(df.index, size=int(N * frac), replace=False)
    df.loc[idx, col] = np.nan

inject_missing("YearBuilt", 0.06)
inject_missing("LotSizeSqFt", 0.08)
inject_missing("SchoolRating", 0.05)
inject_missing("Bathrooms", 0.04)
inject_missing("GarageSpaces", 0.05)
inject_missing("CrimeRatePer1000", 0.03)
inject_missing("Condition", 0.04)

# A few outliers / entry errors to catch during cleaning
outlier_idx = rng.choice(df.index, size=8, replace=False)
df.loc[outlier_idx[:3], "LivingAreaSqFt"] = df.loc[outlier_idx[:3], "LivingAreaSqFt"] * 15  # fat-finger entry
df.loc[outlier_idx[3:5], "YearBuilt"] = 2101  # impossible future year
df.loc[outlier_idx[5:7], "Bathrooms"] = -2     # negative value error
df.loc[outlier_idx[7], "SalePrice_CAD"] = 8000  # implausibly low price

# A handful of exact duplicate rows (common real-world issue)
dup_rows = df.sample(5, random_state=1)
df = pd.concat([df, dup_rows], ignore_index=True)

# Shuffle final row order
df = df.sample(frac=1, random_state=3).reset_index(drop=True)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# Save
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
out_path = "/home/claude/real_estate_project/data/real_estate_raw.csv"
df.to_csv(out_path, index=False)
print(f"Saved {len(df)} rows to {out_path}")
print(df.isna().sum())

The main goal is to leverage the historical data in order to make better data-driven decisions. Looking for different predictive/clustering use-cases to maximise the revenue, reduce the costs and understand the portfolio.

In order to prepare the data for injection into models and ensure predictions for the target variable (SalePrice) with good accuracy, we need first to understand our data and clean it.

Our dataset contains a set of variables describing residential properties. It's also a large, complex dataset that contains 2,505 rows and 20 columns (features), and our target variable is SalePrice (numeric variable).

Find the list of variables with missing data and number of missing values

I loaded our data as a CSV file called "real_estate_raw", then I counted the missing values in every column and last printed a sorted list of only the columns that have missing data for better visualization.

Data Preparation for modeling:

  1. Check datatypes for each column
  2. Identify numeric columns and build distribution histograms
  3. Identify categorical columns and generate frequency distribution histogram
  4. Perform imputations for missing values in numeric fields and cap any unusual extreme outliers (if any)
  5. Outliers detection

Datatypes

We used df.info() to reveal the types of our features in the dataframe (float/integer/object) [numeric or categorical].

Numeric columns

Numeric Column Features: ['Bedrooms', 'Bathrooms', 'LivingAreaSqFt', 'LotSizeSqFt', 'YearBuilt', 'GarageSpaces', 'HasBasement', 'HasPool', 'RenovationYear', 'SchoolRating', 'CrimeRatePer1000', 'DistanceToDowntownKm', 'DaysOnMarket', 'SalePrice_CAD', 'AnnualPropertyTaxCAD']. Total numeric columns: 15.

The target variable Saleprice is a continuous numerical variable that has a unimodal and right-skewed shape, the bulk of properties cluster is in the lower-to-mid price range, with a long tail stretching toward higher values. The peak is concentrated around 600 000 and 700 000 CAD, which is where the tallest bar sits.

Most properties fall between roughly 250 000 and 1 000 000 CAD, with the density dropping off steadily beyond that. Then, we can see that a long right tail extends out to about 1 750 000 CAD, representing a smaller number of high-value properties, likely larger homes, premium neighborhoods or luxury segments in the portfolio. And in the left side, there is a thin tail near 0 to 250 000 CAD, suggesting few very low-priced properties.

Because of the right skew, the mean Saleprice is pulled higher than the median.

To sum up, this kind of skew is addressed with a log transformation before feeding into models like linear regression, though tree-based models like random forest is robust to it as is.

Categorical columns

Categorical Column Features: ['Condition', 'Neighborhood', 'PropertyType']. Total categorical columns : 3

In this script, in order to understand the shape of our data, the skewness and the presence of outliers, I generated the distribution plots / frequency histograms, for the 3 categorical features (I excluded PropertyID and SaleDate, as they are more temporal/identifier data), and finally I applied a different color to each plot for visual distinction.

Condition
  • Bars sorted in descending order of frequency, dominated by "Good" (over 1 000 properties), roughly 60% more than the next category.
  • "Fair" is second (650), "Excellent" third (470), and "Poor" is the smallest (200).
  • Most properties in the portfolio are in decent-to-average condition; very few are at either extreme (Excellent or Poor).
Neighborhood
  • 11 categories, also sorted descending. "Le Plateau-Mont-Royal" clearly leads (330), noticeably ahead of the rest.
  • A cluster of neighborhoods (Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie, NDG, Laval, Ville-Marie/Downtown, Verdun, Griffintown) sit in a fairly tight mid-range (225–255).
  • "Ahuntsic-Cartierville," "Longueuil," "Westmount," "Outremont," and "Saint-Laurent" form a lower tier (130–180).
  • The distribution has a longer, more gradual decline compared to Condition, more evenly spread across categories rather than one or two categories dominating.
PropertyType
  • 6 categories, again sorted descending. "Condo" dominates (870), roughly double the next category.
  • "Detached" and "Duplex" are close to each other (390–400).
  • "Townhouse," "Semi-Detached," and "Triplex" form the smallest group (260–300).
  • This mirrors typical urban housing stock, where condos are the most common property type and multi-unit/detached homes are comparatively rarer.

Imputation & Outlier Capping

To handle missing values in the numeric variables, I applied a deterministic imputation approach using the median, replacing missing entries in RenovationYear, LotSizeSqFt, YearBuilt, SchoolRating, GarageSpaces, Bathrooms, and CrimeRatePer1000 with each column's respective median value. The median was chosen over the mean because it is robust to outliers, performs well with skewed distributions, and it's widely used for variables such as prices, sales amounts, and surface areas.

Instead of deleting the outliers, I used the IQR method to reduce their extreme influence:

Lower Bound = Q1 − 1.5 × IQR
Upper Bound = Q3 + 1.5 × IQR

After checking the dataset and the missing values in the Condition variable, I found that the NaN values don't correspond to a specific SalePrice range, they span properties as low as 157 300 CAD and as high as 1 452 200 CAD. This means replacing the missing values with the mode wouldn't provide reliable information, and removing the affected rows wasn't a good option either. Since these missing values represent only around 4% of the data, I decided to keep them as an explicit "Unknown" category.

Missing values Verification after the imputation

Outliers detection

SalePrice_CAD: The IQR method identified 29 upper outliers. Further investigation showed that approximately 55% of these observations are located in Westmount, 34% in Outremont, 3% in each of Griffintown, Le Plateau-Mont-Royal and Ville-Marie (Downtown). Comparing sale prices by neighborhoods suggests that the flagged values reflect the concentration of high-value properties in these neighborhoods (most higher sale price average) rather than data-quality errors. Therefore, these observations were retained rather than capped.

Bathrooms: Two properties show fewer than -0.45 bathrooms, which is statistically impossible and clearly points to a data quality issue rather than a legitimate outlier. On the upper end, 25 properties exceed 4.75 bathrooms; further investigation showed that these properties have a LotSizeSqFt ranging from 4 506 to 15 141, consistent with larger properties that would reasonably have more bathrooms.

LotSizeSqFt: Only one property has a lot size exceeding 17 715 sqft. On closer inspection, 31% of properties show LotSizeSqFt = 0, which initially appeared to represent missing or unrecorded data. However, cross-checking these zero-value observations against PropertyType revealed that all of them correspond to "Condo" listings, confirming that a LotSizeSqFt of 0 is correct for this property type, rather than a data quality issue.

LivingAreaSqFt: 3 properties have a living area exceeding 5 312 sq ft. Upon inspection, their sale prices don't align coherently with that living area size.

YearBuilt: the IQR method identifies 2 observations as outliers, which requires an investigation. After looking at the YearBuilt distribution, the 2 outliers are: 2101.

RenovationYear: No outliers were detected here, but the results suggest that at least 75% of the values are 2003.

DistanceToDowntownKm: The IQR method flags a large number of observations as falling outside the statistical range. However, after cross-checking these distances against their corresponding neighborhoods, the values were found to be statistically valid. The minimum is 0 and the maximum is 22.

CrimeRatePer1000: 92 values exceed 27.95, which is a substantial number. However, after cross-checking these values against their corresponding neighborhoods, they were concentrated in the downtown neighborhood which makes them valid.

DaysOnMarket: 34 properties that stayed on the market for more than 73 days and this is not an error, some properties could legitimately remain on the market for 100, 200, or even more days.

Outliers capping (IQR method)

Outlier detection was performed using the IQR method. For each numerical variable, the lower and upper statistical bounds were calculated as Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR, respectively. Some variables produced negative lower bounds (Bathrooms, LotSizeSqFt, and LivingAreaSqFt). These values are statistical thresholds generated by the IQR formula and do not represent valid domain values. Therefore, the flagged observations were reviewed individually and manually corrected where necessary, rather than being capped at physically impossible negative values.

From all previous observations, we can tell that Random Forest is the right call over Linear regression, for these reasons:

  • Skewed target: Saleprice is right skewed (unimodal, long tail). Linear regression assumes normally distributed residuals so we'd need a log-transformation to make it viable. While Random Forest makes no distributional assumption on the target.
  • Mixed feature types: We have 15 numeric and 3 categorical features. Random Forest handles this natively without needing feature scaling.

In this case, Principal Component Analysis isn't necessary, since we don't have a large enough number of variables to warrant dimensionality reduction.

Using 3 core Python libraries: pandas for data handling, scikit-learn for the train/test split function and the Random Forest model itself, and NumPy for numerical operations, I split the dataset into training and testing sets to prepare it for the Random Forest Regression model. This step is essential to evaluate the model on data it hasn't seen during training, avoiding an overly optimistic estimate of its performance.

Predictive modeling using Random Forest

The Random Forest model achieved an R² of 0.9107 on the test set, indicating that approximately 91.1% of the variance in SalePrice_CAD is explained by the model.

On average, our model's price predictions are off by about 76 491 CAD from the actual sale price since RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) = 76491.0668. This value alone doesn't tell if that's a lot or a little, that's why we need to compare it to the typical price range in our data.

The RMSE represents approximately 11.33% of the mean sale price, indicating a relatively moderate prediction error compared with the overall price level.

RMSE is sensitive to large errors. In order to have a much better picture, I calculated the MAE (Mean Absolute Error):

On average, the difference between the actual and the predicted sale price is about 59 000 CAD, it represents 8.7% of the average sale price.

So, to understand where our random forest model makes its largest errors, we need to analyze the residuals distribution.

The residual analysis shows that the model has a relatively small overall bias, with a mean residual of approximately -5,307 CAD, indicating a slight tendency to overestimate sale prices. However, the residuals exhibit substantial dispersion, with a standard deviation of approximately 76 383 CAD. The largest residuals range from -195,311 CAD to +350,251 CAD, indicating that the model can produce substantial errors for some properties / large individual errors. The larger positive residual suggests that the model tends to underestimate certain high-priced properties.

Investigate the properties corresponding to the large errors

The investigation of the 10 observations with the largest absolute residuals revealed that most of the largest errors were positive, indicating that the model tended to underestimate the sale prices of several high-value properties. For instance, the largest underestimation reached 350 251 CAD for a property in Westmount, while several other properties with actual sale prices above 1 million CAD were underestimated by more than 200 000 CAD.

The observations were mainly located in Westmount, Outremont, Le Plateau-Mont-Royal and Griffintown, suggesting that the model may have difficulty capturing certain high-value properties within these neighborhoods. However, large negative residuals were also observed, indicating that the model doesn't systematically underestimate all expensive properties.

Model improvement

The previous findings suggest that some property-specific or location-specific factors may not be fully captured by the available predictors. In order to evaluate which variables are contributing the most to the sale price predictions, I used the model's built-in feature_importances_ attribute. It ranks the input variables based on how much they reduce impurity across all decision trees.

The results show that AnnualPropertyTaxCAD alone accounts for 89% of the Random Forest's feature importance, over 40 times more than the next highest feature: LivingAreaSqFt at 2.2%, which is an extreme concentration. As a matter of fact, property tax is typically calculated as a percentage of assessed value, so it's likely acting as a proxy for SalePrice_CAD, rather than an independent predictor.

In order to confirm it, I calculated the correlation coefficient:

The scatterplot shows a strong, near-linear relationship between AnnualPropertyTaxCAD and SalePrice_CAD, consistent with the 0.937 correlation coefficient. Points cluster tightly along the diagonal at lower tax values, while the spread widens at higher values. A single outlier near AnnualPropertyTaxCAD (around 9000) with a SalePrice_CAD = 0 stands apart from the overall pattern, which reflects a data anomaly.

Overall, this visual pattern reinforces that AnnualPropertyTaxCAD behaves more like a proxy for SalePrice_CAD than an independent predictor.

Removing the leaking features and rebuilding the model

Model R² RMSE
With AnnualPropertyTaxCAD0.910776,491.07 CAD
Without AnnualPropertyTaxCAD0.8169109,506.61 CAD

After dropping AnnualPropertyTaxCAD, R² dropped from 0.9107 to 0.8169, and RMSE rose from 76 491 to 109 507 CAD, which confirms the leakage story. The model is now learning from genuinely independent features rather than a proxy of the target.

Cross-Validation

Across 5 different training/validation splits, the Random Forest has an average R² of 0.8137.

The Random Forest achieved a mean cross-validated R² of 0.8137, compared with the R² of 0.8169 on the held-out test set. So there is no major discrepancy between the cross-validation performance and the test performance. So, the model's predictive performance is relatively stable and there is no evidence of overfitting.

Hyperparameter tuning

Using RandomizedSearchCV, the optimized Random Forest configuration shows that 30 hyperparameter combinations × 5 folds = 150 model fits were performed to determine the best configuration.

The tuning process selected 500 trees, indicating that a relatively large ensemble provided the best cross-validated performance among the tested values.

A maximum tree depth of 20 was selected, providing sufficient complexity to capture nonlinear relationships while limiting excessive tree growth.

The model selected max_features=0.5, meaning that half of the available predictors are randomly considered at each split, increasing tree diversity and potentially reducing correlation between trees.

A minimum of five observations was required to split a node, providing some regularization and reducing the risk of overly specific tree structures (if a node contains only 4 observations, it cannot be split further).

Hyperparameter tuning resulted in a modest improvement in predictive performance. The R² increased from 0.8169 to 0.8233, while RMSE decreased from approximately 109,507 CAD to 107,566 CAD. This indicates that the optimized Random Forest provides slightly better predictive accuracy than the baseline model, although the improvement remains relatively limited.

Gradient Boosting Model

The Gradient Boosting model is better on this test split. The model explains roughly 86.6% of the variability in SalePrice_CAD. This is a meaningful improvement compared with Random Forest's 82.3%.

There is about a 13% reduction in RMSE (107,566 CAD against 93,638 CAD) and a 15.9% reduction in MAE (80,998 CAD against 68,113 CAD).

5-fold Cross-validation Gradient Boosting

Residuals analysis

The model has a small overall tendency toward overprediction, based on the mean residual (-3105 CAD) and the median (-10,676 CAD). Also, the maximum residual (483,250 CAD) shows that the model underpredicted some high-value properties, that's why I calculated the error by price range to determine whether the model's performance deteriorates as the properties prices increase.

The model performs very well overall (R² = 0.9080), but its predictive accuracy is less reliable for high-priced properties.
Residual analysis indicates that prediction errors are concentrated among higher-priced properties, particularly in the 1M–1.5M CAD segment, where the model tends to underestimate sale prices. This suggests that additional features capturing property-specific and luxury-market characteristics could further improve predictions.

Residual and feature importance analyses identified high-value properties as the main source of prediction errors and highlighted living area and proximity to downtown as the strongest predictors.

Property segmentation using K-means and Elbow method

1-Import the data

We imported the cleaned data used for prediction earlier, it contains 2506 records and 20 variables including the target variable. However, we removed the target variable (SalePrice_CAD) from the clustering analysis in order to use it later for properties clusters profiling.

2-Select the clustering characteristics

The clustering characteristics were chosen deliberately to identify the property segmentation. The feature DaysOnMarket was removed because it represents a market outcome more than intrinsic property feature. The variables were separated later into numerical , categorical and binary ones for standardization.

3- Check the selected variables before clustering ( summary statistics, missing data )

The summary statistics above shows the 50% percentile ( Median) ,the 75th percentile and the maximum of each property feature. Living Area sqft and Lot size sqft show a substantial dispersion: 50% of properties have a living area size below 2224 sqft while the maximum is 27 495 sqft, this very large gap suggests important variation in living area size and indicates that there are some large properties that could constitute a cluster on their own.

The missing values investigation indicates that all of them were properly handled during the data preparation section.

4- One-hot encoding of categorical variables

We identified the numerical variables, the binary variables ( HasBasement and HasPool) and the categorical variables ( Neighborhood, Property type and condition ).

The categorical variables were encoded using One-Hot Encoding in order to standardize them in the next section.

5- Standardize numerical and categorical variables
6-Combine all the variables
7- K-means clustering /identify the optimal number of clusters: Highest CH Score

The optimal number of clusters was evaluated using the Calinski-Harabasz (CH) index. The score reached its maximum value at K=2 (524.88) and decreased consistently for higher values of K. In order to dig deeper into the segmentation analysis, we used the Elbow method too.

8- The Elbow method

The elbow plot shows that the inertia (how close the records are to the center of their cluster) decreases as the number of clusters K increases.

The Elbow point appears at k=2, after that point the curve is noticeably flatter.

9- Cluster Profiling (K= 2 clusters )

Combining the k-means clustering and the Elbow method suggests that the properties are grouped into 2 homogenous / compacted clusters, each segment contains :

Cluster 0 : 1163 properties
Cluster 1: 1342 properties

There are some characteristics that distinguish the first group from the second one.

The strongest characteristics separating the clusters are related to property size :

  • Cluster 1 has roughly twice as many bedrooms ( 2 bedrooms on average in cluster 0 against 4 in cluster 1)
  • Cluster 1 has also more bathrooms ( 2 bathrooms vs 3)
  • Cluster 1 properties are much larger ( 1392 sqft vs 3019 sqft)
  • Cluster 1 has much larger lots
  • Cluster 1 is considerably more expensive ( On average 535 599 CAD vs 788 097 CAD)

The Cluster 0 contains Condo-oriented properties ( 73.9% condos, 10.1% townhouses) while Cluster 1 groups larger residential properties such as duplexes, detached houses and triplexes (28.8% Duplex, 23.5% Detached , 18.7% triplex .. and almost no condos)

Other variables don't distinguish the clusters much : YearBuilt ( Almost identical , around 1971), Garage spaces ( identical), school rating (almost identical). The neighborhood distributions are fairly similar

The segmentation is driven primarily by property size and property type rather than by location, crime rate, or distance to downtown

Pipeline Construction and Model Integration

The model provides an automated approach to estimate the property sale price in Montreal, based on features such as location and neighborhood attributes. With an R² of approximately 91%, the model can support property valuation, pricing analysis and market segmentation. However, the residual analysis indicates that predictions are less reliable for some high-value properties, therefore, the model is considered as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for professional valuation.

I developed and optimized a real-estate price prediction model, compared multiple machine-learning approaches, validated its generalization using cross-validation and an unseen test set, diagnosed its remaining errors, identified the key price drivers, and packaged the final model into a reusable prediction pipeline that can support data-driven property valuation and pricing decisions.
